Pregnancy

Muscle rubs and pain patches during pregnancy

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A cream or patch may seem like a simple way to ease a sore back, but medicine applied to the skin is not automatically suitable during pregnancy. Show a pharmacist or maternity clinician the exact product before using it. The ingredients, pregnancy stage, amount and area of application all matter.

Start with the ingredient list

Brands such as Icy Hot sell several formulations. A product may contain menthol, methyl salicylate, lidocaine or another ingredient, sometimes in combination. Advice for one tube or patch does not necessarily apply to another carrying a similar name.

A cooling or warming feeling describes the sensation on the skin, not proof that a product is safe for the baby. Topical products can be absorbed into the body, and using more, covering a large area or adding heat can change exposure.

Keep the box or photograph the active ingredients and strength. Tell the pharmacist how many weeks pregnant you are, where you want to apply it, other medicines you use and any aspirin or medicine allergies.

Menthol and camphor are counterirritants: they create a cooling or warming sensation that can distract from pain. That sensation does not identify which muscle or joint is causing pain, and formulations may contain other medicines.

Methyl salicylate and wintergreen need particular care

Methyl salicylate is found in wintergreen oil and some muscle rubs. It is related to aspirin, but a concentrated rub is not equivalent to a small amount of flavouring in food. Do not use essential-oil concentrates or homemade mixtures as substitutes for a checked medicine.

Pregnancy safety information for these products is limited. UK teratology advice considers ordinary manufacturer-directed exposure to some muscle rubs unlikely to cause problems, while advising precaution about wintergreen-containing products after twenty weeks. Labels and formulations vary, so this is not blanket permission to use every product.

If you have an aspirin or salicylate allergy, tell the professional checking the product. Absence of an allergy does not by itself establish pregnancy safety. Prescribed low-dose aspirin for a pregnancy indication is a separate treatment; do not stop it because of a warning about a muscle rub.

Anti-inflammatory gels have pregnancy restrictions too

Some gels contain an NSAID such as diclofenac. Skin application does not remove the pregnancy precautions. Diclofenac gel labelling warns about fetal kidney effects and low amniotic fluid from around twenty weeks, with additional fetal circulation concerns later in pregnancy.

Do not start an NSAID gel at twenty weeks or later unless a clinician specifically directs it; use later in pregnancy may need to be avoided entirely. Earlier use also deserves a product-specific check. A medicine does not become generally safe just because the first trimester has ended.

If a clinician recommends a particular treatment, follow the agreed amount, area and duration. Do not combine several pain gels or patches, or add an oral anti-inflammatory, without checking the plan.

Protect your skin and avoid heat combinations

If a product has been approved for you, follow its own directions. Do not apply it to broken or irritated skin, under a tight dressing, or near the eyes or other sensitive areas unless the instructions specifically allow it. Wash your hands after application.

Never place a heating pad, hot-water bottle or other heat source over a medicated pain rub or patch. Serious burns have occurred with topical pain products, and heat may also increase absorption.

Stop using the product and seek medical advice for significant pain, swelling or blistering where it was applied. A strong burning sensation is not evidence that it is working better. Accidental swallowing needs immediate poison-service or medical advice.

Consider comfort measures and assessment

Try supported sitting, changing position, comfortable footwear and gentle movement within your maternity team’s advice. Pregnancy-related pain is not your fault, and pushing through painful exercise is not a requirement. A physiotherapist can tailor movement and support for back or pelvic pain.

A wrapped cool pack or gentle local warmth may help some muscular discomfort when used without a medicated product. Protect the skin and avoid overheating. Ask about pregnancy-qualified massage if it feels helpful; complementary treatments are not guaranteed to work or automatically risk-free.

When medicine is needed, paracetamol is generally the first choice for mild-to-moderate pain in pregnancy, used according to professional advice and the label. Ongoing pain still needs a cause and a plan rather than repeated self-treatment.

A supportive chair and pillow can reduce strain while sitting or resting. Walking, water exercise or gentle stretches may suit you; stop movements that worsen pain and ask for an individual plan. Stable low-heeled footwear can be more comfortable as balance changes. Massage or acupuncture should be discussed with the maternity team and provided by someone experienced in pregnancy.

Do not cover up warning symptoms

Contact maternity care promptly for new significant back pain with bleeding, leaking fluid, contractions, fever, painful urination or pain under the ribs. Severe pain, weakness or loss of sensation in the legs or genital area needs urgent assessment.

If you already used a rub once, do not assume harm has occurred. Keep the product details and ask for an assessment of the actual exposure, especially after repeated use, a large application or use later in pregnancy. That is more useful than treating all creams as equally safe or equally dangerous.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

FDA and product labelling warn that NSAID medicines can affect fetal kidneys and amniotic fluid from around 20 weeks; a gel still requires pregnancy-specific advice.

BUMPS and NHS guidance support checking the exact product and using appropriate comfort measures or analgesia while investigating persistent pain.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you prepare product details and symptom questions. A pharmacist or maternity clinician should assess the ingredient, amount and pregnancy stage.

When to seek help

Do not heat medicated patches or rubs. Skin blistering, accidental ingestion or pregnancy pain with bleeding, fever, contractions or fluid leakage needs prompt help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The active ingredient matters more than the brand name or the word “topical.”
  • Check methyl salicylate and NSAID products carefully, particularly after twenty weeks.
  • Never combine a medicated rub or patch with a heating pad.
  • Persistent or severe pain needs assessment, not simply a stronger rub.

Frequently asked questions

Is every Icy Hot product the same?

No. Different formulations can contain different active ingredients and strengths. Check the exact package.

Are over-the-counter medicines generally safe after the first trimester?

No. Some important medicine risks occur later in pregnancy. Timing remains part of the assessment.

Does one accidental use mean the baby has been harmed?

Not necessarily. Ask a pharmacist or maternity clinician to assess the product, amount, timing and frequency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
